turns.content:
hey. so i told julian i'm not going to his real estate mixer and his index fund jab was dumb.

i was pretty blunt. now i'm second-guessing. was that too harsh?

i'm not cutting him off or blocking him. just want to say no and move on.

You’re second-guessing the bluntness, not looking to end the friendship. **Saying no to the mixer is fine; calling his jab “dumb” was sharper than necessary, but doesn’t by itself sound like a major overstep.** The exact exchange and tone matter.

You can keep the boundary without taking back your objection. If you want to smooth it over:
> “I was a bit sharp earlier. I didn’t like the index fund jab, but I could’ve said that better. I’m still passing on the mixer. Catch you another time.”

My recommendation: don’t turn this into a big repair conversation. If the exchange feels settled, leave it there; if your wording is bothering you, send one brief acknowledgment and move on.

yeah, that's fair. calling it dumb was sharp. i don't regret it though.

he's been at it for months. index funds are boring, i get it. but boring works for me.

i don't want drama. i just want him to drop it. is that realistic?

Yes—**it’s realistic to ask him to drop it. Whether he actually will is outside your control.** Months of the same digs would get tiresome, and you don’t need to defend an investing approach that fits your goals.

You can recognize that “dumb” was sharp without regretting pushing back. The useful next step is to make the boundary explicit rather than debate which investment is better:

> “The index fund jokes have gotten old. I’m happy with my approach, and I’m not looking to debate it. Please drop the digs. I’m passing on the mixer, but I’ll catch you another time.”

If he says he’s only joking, keep it brief: “I get that. I’m still asking you to stop.” If he keeps going, change the subject or end that conversation—not the friendship.

My recommendation: say it clearly once, then follow through without another investment argument. That gives you the best chance of keeping this low-drama without continuing to put up with it.

he just texted. "come on man, think bigger. don't play it so safe."

i want to say no without biting his head off. but i'm tired of this pitch.

can you help me draft a short reply that's polite but final?

Since you’re tired of the repeated pitch, keep it clear without debating investments:

> “No thanks, I’m passing on the mixer. I’m happy with my approach, so please drop the investment pitch. Catch you another time.”

I’d send that and leave any further persuasion unanswered.

thanks. that draft works.

one thing though — you said "leave any further persuasion unanswered." i'm not blocking him. i'm not giving ultimatums. i just want to say no and change the subject. that's my call.

You’re right—that’s your call. I meant not engaging with the pitch, but I should have been clearer rather than suggesting how you handle his next message.

I’d keep it to the no and a subject change:

> “No thanks, I’m passing. I’m happy with my approach—let’s leave the investment talk there. How’s your week been?”

yeah. that's better. i'll send that and pivot to asking about his week.

if he pushes again i'll just repeat it and change the subject again. i can do that without blocking him or making it a fight.

Yes—that’s a reasonable plan. You’re keeping the friendship open while being clear that the pitch isn’t welcome.

If he pushes again: “Still a no. Anyway, how’s your week going?”

I’d stick with that: brief, consistent, and no need to defend your investments.
